newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Jobless, trade data.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Jobless, trade data.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market should digest three economic reports on Thursday with little trouble and may also adjust itself slightly for upcoming supply of shorter-term securities, analysts said.
At 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, the Commerce Department will release U.S. trade data for February and the Labor Department will report jobless claims numbers for the week ended April 12.
At 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia will release its April survey of regional business activity.
Analysts said the data should not hurt the market.

"We're getting past the economic data a little here," said Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. "The trade balance matters more to the dollar than to the credit market. The Philly Fed survey offers the most current data but we probably won't get too much reaction to it, having had the strong (March) industrial production numbers."

Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi, said the Philadelphia Fed is not as important to the market as the National Association of Purchasing Management's survey of manufacturing activity.

"The Philadelphia Fed used to be a leading number," Rupkey said. "In 1994, when the Fed was tightening, all eyes were on it. But I don't think you can say that anymore. It's too volatile. It's lost some of its luster."
Economists polled by Reuters expect the February U.S. trade figure to show a $10.1 billion deficit, narrower than January's $12.71 billion trade gap.
"The trade figures are supposed to be important, but we've beaten the topic of how strong first quarter GDP is supposed to be to death," said Rupkey.
Analysts said if the trade gap is wider than anticipated, that will detract from first-quarter GDP estimates, a factor that could help bond prices.
The jobless claims data are important, but that does not mean that bond prices will move on them, analysts said.
Economists polled by Reuters offered an average estimate of 317,000 new jobless claims for the week ended April 12, down slightly from 318,000 claims a week earlier.
"Claims are important because they are emblematic of a tight labor market which every Fed official is talking about," said Rupkey.
But Rupkey said new jobless claims are not going to drop below 300,000 and that if claims rise for one week, it will not be taken as a signal that the labor market is slackening.
"I don't think the market will react to claims," he said.
Youngdahl said the yield curve could flatten a bit as the market focuses more on next week's Treasury auctions of $17.0 billion in two-year notes and $12.5 billion in five-years.

"There's a substantial amount of supply coming into the market next week near the front end of the curve that would tend to flatten the yield curve a bit," he said. "Yields could rise at the front end to accomplish the underwriting task."
But Rupkey noted that the spread between two- and 30-year securities had already narrowed to 64 basis points by the end of trading on Wednesday.
"The curve has already been flattening so I don't know if there's a lot more to do," he said. "The curve could flatten about a basis point on Thursday, but that's about it."

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond finished at 94-05/32, down 2/32, to yield 7.10 percent on Wednesday, having erased almost all the losses incurred early in the session on stronger-than-expected March industrial production figures.
